When schools and workplaces operate as usual, many people can’t make it to the polls, can’t take time off, or can’t balance voting with hourly shifts and caregiving duties. A holiday would remove that friction and make voting easier for everyone.

It also reframes voting as a civic celebration rather than a stressful chore. That matters: treating Election Day as a day for democracy elevates the importance of civic participation.

Public support is broad—71% of Democrats and 59% of Republicans support making Election Day a holiday—and globally this isn’t radical: 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays, showing it can be done effectively without undermining election integrity.

Election Day as a national holiday sounds appealing, but it’s not the most reliable or equitable fix—and by itself it won’t solve the real access problems.

First, a federal holiday doesn’t guarantee paid time off for most voters. While a government closure might give some people flexibility, federal law doesn’t require private employers to treat holidays as paid or to give workers time to vote. In retail, food service, gig work, and other hourly roles—where low-income workers are overrepresented—many people would still have to work or would still lose income if they take time to vote. So the people most affected by scheduling constraints may not actually benefit much from a holiday.

Second, even if an election day holiday creates more opportunity for some, it doesn’t directly address the bottlenecks that stop voters: registration issues, ID rules and administrative barriers, limited early/absentee options, long lines, and last-minute disruptions. Making state-level reforms that directly expand access is more dependable than changing the calendar.

Third, the research premise that “an election holiday alone” is an effective turnout strategy is weak compared to other reforms. Turnout rises when policies reduce frictions in the voting process—automatic voter registration, better early voting/absentee access, and laws requiring time off or streamlined voting procedures—rather than when we simply declare the day a holiday.

Bottom line: If the goal is to boost turnout and remove barriers, we should prioritize reforms that ensure actual time and administrative access—like state laws requiring employer time-off for voting, automatic voter registration, and expanded early/absentee voting—rather than relying on a national holiday that may not translate into meaningful paid freedom for low-income workers.

That reduces the number of voters who must choose between work, caregiving, and voting—even if it doesn’t solve every case.

Second, agent 2 frames “real access problems” as if the only access solution is paperwork or administrative expansions. Yet scheduling barriers are their own access problem. Even when registration and early voting are improved, many voters still need a guaranteed window—especially for people who can’t use early/absentee options well (caregiving schedules, jobs with unpredictable hours, limited ability to arrange transportation or paperwork). A holiday creates a common, shared opportunity that reduces last-minute constraints.

Third, agent 2 claims the most affected groups may not benefit because some hourly workers still must work. That objection doesn’t defeat the policy; it clarifies implementation needs (e.g., pairing the holiday with stronger requirements for time to vote). But the existence of imperfect coverage doesn’t mean the policy has no effect. In the same way, expanding early/absentee access isn’t perfect, yet it’s still worthwhile.
